title: Upali the householder
hook: a supporter of the Jain monks changes teachers; the Buddha tells him to keep feeding them

segments.voice: Yesterday: Jivaka, and your line, know your food. Did you pause before one bite and think of where it came from? Today, the end of a week, and a gift that keeps going. Day four hundred forty-eight.

In the town of Nalanda lives Upali, a wealthy householder and a devoted supporter of the Niganthas, the community of ascetics around the teacher Jains know as Mahavira. His house has fed their monks for years. One day a Nigantha monk comes back from talking with the Buddha, and Upali, confident, says: let me go and debate this Gotama myself. I'll drag him around like a strong man drags a ram by its fleece. His teacher agrees. Today: Upali the householder.
screen: `NALANDA. A GENEROUS HOUSEHOLDER.` → `A SUPPORTER OF THE NIGANTHAS.` → `LET ME DEBATE HIM MYSELF.`

segments.voice: This is the fifty-sixth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, the discourse to Upali. The question is: of body, speech and mind, which kind of action does the most harm? Upali's side says body. The Buddha says mind, the intention behind it all. They talk, with examples on both sides, and by the end Upali is persuaded. He asks to become the Buddha's lay follower. And here the Buddha does something surprising. He doesn't welcome him at once. He says: investigate thoroughly, Upali. It's good for a well-known man like you to think carefully first. Upali, moved, asks again. Then the Buddha says the line this story is remembered for. Your family has long been a well-spring for the Nigantha monks. You should keep giving to them when they come. Upali is struck. He'd heard that the Buddha told people to give only to him and his disciples. And here the Buddha is telling him to keep feeding the monks of the community he has just left. Upali says this makes him even more glad. This is how the Buddhist text tells the story; Jain tradition has its own texts and its own accounts of that time, and the two don't tell it the same way. But the Buddha's instruction speaks for itself. Changing your mind doesn't cancel your kindness. Old bonds of generosity are worth keeping. Look back at this week: Mara named at the door, the thicket of people, eleven doors, a hen, a bare bone, Jivaka's question. Today: a gift that keeps going.
screen: `BODY, SPEECH OR MIND: WHICH HARMS MOST?` · `INVESTIGATE THOROUGHLY FIRST` · `KEEP GIVING TO THE NIGANTHA MONKS` · `THIS WEEK: A GIFT THAT KEEPS GOING` · then, large: `KEEP GIVING TO THEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep one old kindness going. Sit, and think of a kindness you used to give that has slipped since something changed: a call to an old friend, a gift to a group you've drifted from, a neighbor you used to check on. Picture them. Notice that the change in your life didn't make them less worthy of kindness. Picture one small way to keep giving. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Upali. A generous man who changed teachers, and was told by his new teacher to keep feeding the monks of his old one. Today's word.
Your line: keep giving to them. Today, keep one old kindness going, even if your life has moved on from where it started. Day four hundred forty-eight.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often cite the Buddha's words to Upali as an example of generosity that doesn't depend on who the recipient follows; dana, giving, is practiced by lay Buddhists toward monastics and toward people in need.

fork.setup: you're the Buddha. a generous, well-known man who has long supported another community asks to become your follower. what do you say first?
options: only if you bring your whole family.
fork.reveal: the Buddha tells Upali to investigate thoroughly. when he asks again, the Buddha accepts, and tells him to keep giving to the Nigantha monks.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit dana: giving, generosity. Upali's house was a well-spring of dana.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about one side winning a convert.
what it means: changing your mind doesn't cancel your kindness; the Buddha tells Upali to keep giving to his old community.

what a scholar hears: the debate turns on danda, 'rods' of body, speech and mind; the Niganthas weigh the bodily most, the Buddha the mental, which shows how central intention (cetana) is in Buddhist teaching on karma.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 56, Upali Sutta (the discourse to Upali)

notes: MN 56 paraphrased: the debate on the three 'rods' (danda), Upali's boast (the ram by its fleece), 'investigate thoroughly', 'your family has long been a well-spring (opana) for the Niganthas', Upali's surprise. Confirm.
